title: AI chatbot serving
brief: Millions of people ask your assistant questions. Each reply takes a GPU several seconds, and GPUs are expensive and sometimes simply unavailable. Keep replies flowing, protect your wallet from abuse, and have a plan for when the GPUs run out.

clarify.q: How long may a reply take?
clarify.a: The first words should appear in about a second. A complete reply may take up to about 14 seconds; during a GPU shortage a few take longer.

clarify.q: What if we run out of GPUs?
clarify.a: Use a hosted model from an outside provider as overflow, at a higher cost per reply. Better a pricier answer than an error.
Yes, so people can come back to them. They are private and encrypted.

clarify.q: Should every question be answered fresh?
clarify.a: No. Very common questions can reuse a saved answer.

notes: A GPU makes about 6 replies per second with batching (approx.).
A hosted model costs about $0.003 per reply (approx.).

Cost if every reply used a hosted model

hints: GPUs are the scarce, expensive part. What can stand in front of them to absorb abuse and repeats?
Add a rate limiter per user, a safety filter, and a semantic cache for repeated questions. Keep a hosted model as overflow.
A partial stream is an observable result. Recovery semantics and charging must be explicit. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Treat GPU time as the precious resource. A per-user limit stops one person eating a thousand replies. A semantic cache reuses answers to common questions. Your own GPUs are the main path, and an outside hosted model is the escape valve for shortages and spikes.

designs.name: Gateway, cache, own GPUs, hosted overflow
designs.why: The limiter and safety filter protect cost and reputation. The semantic cache removes repeats. Own GPUs carry the base load cheaply, and the gateway falls back to the hosted model when they are full or unavailable.

tradeoffs: A semantic cache saves GPU time on repeats but can return a slightly different answer to a similar question.
Own GPUs cost less per reply at steady load. A hosted model costs more per reply but needs no buying ahead.
A strict per-user limit saves money and protects others, but may annoy heavy users.
A smaller model answers faster and cheaper, with lower quality. Gateways often route easy questions to it.
editorial.realWorld: A mid-size model produces about 2,500 tokens a second per GPU with batching and a reply is around 400 tokens, so one GPU does a few replies a second. A GPU is roughly $2 to $4 an hour (approx.).

correctness.prompt: AI chatbot serving: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Admit generation within token and GPU budgets and recover interrupted replies explicitly. Request count hides large differences in compute and memory demand. Waiting consumes the latency budget and can create an unbounded bill. A partial stream is an observable result. Recovery semantics and charging must be explicit.
